sweep_summary: One item only (Ávila 2018 MA thesis, Instituto Caro y Cuervo). Located via the ICC Koha catalogue (biblionumber 110894) whose 856 field points to the open EPrints record 1346; the 16.8 MB scanned PDF (CC BY-NC-ND) was downloaded to and logged in there. The thesis is an acoustic vowel-formant study of four Mɨnɨka speakers in Bogotá and explicitly excludes stress from its analysis (p. 29); its word-list annex is unmarked for stress. Its literature chapter (pp. 9, 17-18) gives a clear second-hand statement, from Minor & Minor 1976 and Gasché 2009a, that Mɨnɨka has a mobile accent on the first or second syllable (never final in words longer than two syllables), fixed under suffixation, with two lexical root classes that Gasché describes as tonal profiles (HH roots shift accent rightward under suffixation: jófo ~ jofóna, íkó ~ ikómo; HL roots keep initial accent: ómoi, síki), plus initial-long-vowel roots keeping initial accent. This refines but does not contradict the catalog's 'lexical' coding based on Minor, Minor & Levinsohn 1982, and does not supersede that first-hand source. Acquisition pointers surfaced by the thesis: Gasché 2009a 'Esbozo gramatical de la lengua huitoto' (DoBeS People of the Center, Nijmegen; archive.mpi.nl could not be reached by automated download to anonymous requests, dobes.mpi.nl/projects/center reachable but corpus needs login) and Minor & Minor 1976 'Fonología del huitoto', Sistemas fonológicos de idiomas colombianos III: 59-67 (SIL sites 403 behind an automated-access block) — both high priority as the likely first-hand statements of the stress rules. search done via Crossref/OpenAlex/Glottolog/ICC Koha and EPrints directly.

new_statements.quote: A nivel suprasegmental, al igual que el nipode, hay presencia de un acento móvil que puede caer en la primera o segunda sílaba cuando la palabra tiene más de dos sílabas, es decir que nunca cae en la última sílaba como ocurre en bue y mika. Sin embargo, cuando a estas palabras se les agrega un sufijo, cualquiera que sea este, el acento queda fijo. Adicionalmente, parece haber un aumento en la intensidad de la voz que acompaña la sílaba acentuada. Gasché (2009a). A este respecto, Gasché (2009a) menciona algunas reglas de acentuación: Las palabras bisílabas tienen dos perfiles tonales: tono alto - tono alto y tono bajo - tono alto, los cuales condicionan la movilidad del acento
new_statements.translation: At the suprasegmental level, as in Nɨpode, there is a mobile accent that can fall on the first or the second syllable when the word has more than two syllables, i.e. it never falls on the last syllable, as in Bue and Mɨka. However, when a suffix, whatever it is, is added to these words, the accent becomes fixed. In addition there seems to be an increase in voice intensity accompanying the accented syllable. Gasché (2009a). In this regard Gasché (2009a) mentions some accentuation rules: disyllabic words have two tonal profiles, high-high and low-high [sic; examples labelled high-low], which condition the mobility of the accent.
new_statements.citation: Ávila, Youlín Yandiria. 2018. Las vocales en sílaba CV orales acentuadas del minika hablado en Bogotá: una descripción fonético-acústica. MA thesis, Instituto Caro y Cuervo, Bogotá (summarising Minor & Minor 1976 and Gasché 2009a, Esbozo gramatical de la lengua huitoto, DoBeS 'People of the Center').
new_statements.reading: Second-hand but explicit: Mɨnɨka word accent is lexically distributed between the first and second syllable of the root (two lexical classes of disyllabic roots, described by Gasché in tonal terms as HH vs HL), shifts to the second syllable under suffixation for one class and stays initial for the other, and is never word-final in longer words; the phonetic cue is intensity. This is consistent with the catalog's 'lexical' coding (Minor, Minor & Levinsohn 1982: accent 'como en español', unpredictable penult vs final in disyllables, marked orthographically) and refines it: the accent window is the first two syllables of the word, and the two-way lexical contrast may be tonal in origin (Gasché). Not a first-hand description: the thesis itself measures only vowel formants and states that it does not discuss stress.

new_statements.quote: En huitoto las palabras se acentúan lo mismo como en español. Al diferirse la pronunciación el acento se marca. Las palabras de dos o tres sílabas que se acentúan en la sílaba penúltima (palabras graves o llanas) no llevan una tilde. Ejemplos: "jofo" casa, "jofomo" a la casa. Las palabras de dos sílabas que se acentúan en la última sílaba (palabras agudas) siempre llevan una tilde. Ejemplos: "jitó" hijo, "nahí" verdadero, "benó" acá. [...] Sin embargo, como en huitoto el acento siempre está en la primera o segunda sílaba, es más fácil describir el acento al mirar las primeras sílabas de una palabra. Esto es especialmente importante cuando una palabra tiene muchas sílabas. Desde luego, éstas sobrepasan las reglas de español para sobreesdrújulas.
new_statements.translation: In Huitoto words are accented the same way as in Spanish. Where the pronunciation differs, the accent is marked. Words of two or three syllables accented on the penultimate syllable (paroxytones) carry no accent mark. Examples: "jofo" house, "jofomo" to the house. Two-syllable words accented on the final syllable (oxytones) always carry an accent mark. Examples: "jitó" son, "nahí" true, "benó" here. [...] However, since in Huitoto the accent is always on the first or the second syllable, it is easier to describe the accent by looking at the first syllables of a word. This is especially important when a word has many syllables. Of course, these go beyond the Spanish rules for proparoxytones.
new_statements.citation: Minor, Eugene E. and Minor, Dorothy A. and Levinsohn, Stephen H. (1982). Gramática pedagógica huitoto. Bogotá: Ministerio de Gobierno. 130 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the catalog's own source: the catalog record (lexical, page-image grade, quote from p. 6) and the existing Ávila 2018 statement (which summarises exactly this passage) rest on it. The independent archive.org scan confirms the quote verbatim against the page image. Agrees with the catalog's lexical coding and with the first-two-syllables window in the Ávila summary; adds the future-tense and plural remarks that accent shifts to the first syllable under certain morphology.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent always falls on the first or the second syllable of the word, however long the word is; which of the two is not predictable from syllable count and is therefore written with a tilde following Spanish conventions (jofo, jófomo vs jitó, nahí, benó; nágarui, ácata, ácataacade, jofómona, benómona). A lexically fixed accent inside a two-syllable left-edge window.
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions stated for the two-syllable window. Morphological notes elsewhere: the negative suffix -ne does not change the accent (p. 16, 'El acento no se cambia'); in the future tense 'el acento siempre se da en la primera sílaba de la palabra' (p. 24; p. 26 before the linker -tɨ-); special plural forms indicating a large quantity are often shorter than the singular 'y por lo general el acento cambia a la primera sílaba de la palabra' (p. 34); demonstrative pronouns with suffixes require the accent to be written on the appropriate syllable (p. 102 of the PDF). No tone is mentioned anywhere in the grammar.
new_statements.identity_note: Minor, Minor & Levinsohn 1982 is explicitly 'Huitoto (dialecto Mɨnɨca)'. Koch-Grünberg 1906 records 'la langue Ouitóto-Káime' collected on the lower Apaporis in March-April 1905 (plus Berner's material); Glottolog files it under mini1256 but the identification of that 1905 lect with modern Mɨnɨka is not asserted in the work. The archive.org 'huitotodiccionario' item checked while hunting the 1987 vocabulary is the 1971 Nɨpode (Muinane) vocabulary, not Mɨnɨka.

new_statements.quote: El acento /´/ es un fonema contrastivo y está acompañado de tono alto: /íθide/ 'hacer daño o mal', /iθíde/ 'cerner'. Cuando el acento de la palabra fonológica cae en la primera vocal de un grupo de vocales, el tono descendente que resulta es un deslizamiento de tono alto a tono bajo [V́.V̀] y puede dar el efecto de un contraste posible de tono. Este es más notable en el dialecto nɨpode [...]. Sin embargo, el acento fonémico se ha basado en la ocurrencia consistente de un acento-tono alto por cada palabra, resultando en un análisis menos complicado. [p. 67, Ortografía:] Se marca el acento cuando no ocurre en la sílaba penúltima.
new_statements.translation: The accent /´/ is a contrastive phoneme and is accompanied by high tone: /íθide/ 'to do harm', /iθíde/ 'to sift'. When the accent of the phonological word falls on the first vowel of a vowel group, the resulting falling tone is a glide from high to low tone [V́.V̀] and can give the effect of a possible tone contrast. This is more noticeable in the Nɨpode dialect [...]. Nevertheless, phonemic accent has been posited on the basis of the consistent occurrence of one accent-high tone per word, which yields a less complicated analysis. [Orthography:] The accent is written when it does not fall on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's lexical coding (Minor, Minor & Levinsohn 1982 'acento como en español', contrastive in disyllables) and with Ávila 2018's second-hand summary (accent on 1st or 2nd syllable, cue intensity/pitch); adds first-hand detail: accent is a contrastive phoneme accompanied by high tone, exactly one per phonological word, penult is the unmarked orthographic position, and a dialect note on Nɨpode. Does not state the 'never final in words of 3+ syllables' window that Ávila reports from Gasché.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent in Mɨnɨka Huitoto is phonemic (lexically contrastive, minimal pair íθide vs iθíde), one accent per phonological word, realised with high pitch on the accented vowel (falling glide over a following vowel). The authors explicitly choose an accent analysis over a tone analysis. Orthographically the accent is marked only when it is NOT on the penult, i.e. penultimate is treated as the default/most frequent position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; one accent-high tone per phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: Possible tone-like contrast on vowel sequences (accent on first vowel of a VV group gives a high-low glide); in the Nɨpode dialect accent+high tone sometimes falls on the second of two like vowels [V̀.V́]. No positional restriction stated beyond the orthographic penult default.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Mɨnɨka (mɨnɨca/'meneca') dialect of Huitoto spoken on the upper Igara-Paraná (Colombia), i.e. exactly mini1256; the 1976 paper adds a passing comparative remark on the Nɨpode dialect (nipo1235).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Only an orthographic convention: the acute accent is written following Spanish rules, i.e. word accent is not predictable from a single fixed position and is marked where Spanish defaults (penult in vowel-final words) would not give it; headwords in the dictionary carry written accents accordingly (e.g. bitíaiɨi, iráizaibite, áillue). No phonological discussion of stress.

sources.quote: El acento /´/ es un fonema contrastivo y está acompañado de tono alto: /íθide/ 'hacer daño o mal', /iθíde/ 'cerner'. Cuando el acento de la palabra fonológica cae en la primera vocal de un grupo de vocales, el tono descendente que resulta es un deslizamiento de tono alto a tono bajo [V́.V̀] y puede dar el efecto de un contraste posible de tono. Este es más notable en el dialecto nɨpode [...]. Sin embargo, el acento fonémico se ha basado en la ocurrencia consistente de un acento-tono alto por cada palabra, resultando en un análisis menos complicado. [p. 67, Ortografía:] Se marca el acento cuando no ocurre en la sílaba penúltima.
